lines.text: In 2013, physicists made a gas with a temperature below absolute zero.
Absolute zero is the floor, minus two hundred and seventy-three point one five degrees. Nothing has ever got there.
But in Munich, about a hundred thousand atoms read minus a few billionths of a kelvin.
And here's the strange part. It isn't colder than zero.
By the standard definition, it's hotter than any positive temperature at all.
As the researchers put it, the scale doesn't end at infinity. It jumps to negative values.
So how can something below zero be hotter than anything above it? The full video ends on it, and it's linked right here.
